item.title: The Rise and Fall of Shanghai’s “Sing-Song Girls”
item.dc:creator: H.M.A. Leow
item.description:
How did celebrated entertainers become associated with a profession increasingly defined by exploitation?

The post The Rise and Fall of Shanghai’s “Sing-Song Girls” appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
item.content:encoded:
Their dalliances with elite men made the tabloids, and their biographies were printed in guidebooks. If the record is to be believed, courtesans were the glamor girls of old Shanghai.

But Chinese sex workers were not all equal in the historical public imagination. Popular discourse held that “courtesans were a source of pleasure and streetwalkers a source of danger” in early twentieth-century Shanghai, notes historian Gail Hershatter, who estimates that as many as one in 19 women in the city worked in the sex trade by the 1940s.

Their story begins with traditional performers—later called shuyu—who, like the geisha of Japan, might engage in liaisons with patrons. The nineteenth century saw the emergence of a new class of sex workers that was “sexually more accessible,” as historian Christian Henriot puts it.

The courtesan demimonde began to lose its luster, which Henriot attributes to the fact that “a status-dominated society was increasingly replaced by a money-dominated society” from the 1860s onward, as social changes drove up the demand for commercial sexual services.

In the twentieth century, a class of entertainers sometimes known in English as “sing-song girls” continued to command prestige. Many had “comparable artistic skills” to those of the shuyu, but charged fixed rates for their sexual services rather than depending on gifts from elite patrons. Despite their singing and storytelling skills, Henriot argues that the sing-song girls were more akin to “common prostitutes” than historical courtesans.

As more women entered the modern workforce, certain occupations—such as tea hostesses or masseuses—also came to involve offering sexual services to supplement their income.

Indeed, Hershatter agrees that “the sing-song girls had been absorbed into a less exalted group” by the 1920s: changsan sex workers. Named after a mahjong tile that means “long three,” the changsan charged three yuan for drinks and three more for overnight company.

Modern Shanghai also attracted sex workers from far and wide, including so-called “American girls”—white women who, despite their moniker, were more likely to be Russian.

Courtesans aside, the sex trade also included women who sold no-frills sex—either in brothels called “salt pork shops” that catered to laborers, or as “pheasants” on the streets. Such women had low social status. Hershatter notes that salt pork shop workers were compared to a dish that “has not only lost the true flavor of meat, but always smells foul.”

As more women entered the modern workforce, certain occupations—such as tea hostesses or masseuses—also came to involve offering sexual services to supplement their income. “[E]ach of these new types of prostitute appropriated some aspect of the older courtesan traditions; but they did so in Westernized dress,” Hershatter writes. “Theirs was a ‘modern’ form of prostitution, with emphasis on functional and efficient delivery of service.”

More to Explore

Regulating Sex Work in Medieval Europe

Livia Gershon
March 2, 2019
When sex work was considered a "necessary evil," legal brothels provided certain protections for the women who worked there.

Amid the increasing commercialization of the sex trade, authors continued to produce guidebooks on courtesans that rank “[a]mong the richest sources on Shanghai prostitution.” With titles like Pictures of the hundred beauties of flowerland, these guidebooks contained information on correct etiquette with courtesans, along with an overview of fees and tips.

Lamenting the supposed loss of a golden age, the authors modeled themselves on classical historians to produce what Hershatter calls a “literature of nostalgia.”

“Just as historians frequently mourned the failure of contemporary rulers to measure up to the sagacious rulers of yore, guidebook authors mourned the decline in entertainment skill, refinement, and classical training of upper-class prostitutes,” she writes.

Though the guidebooks recommended patronizing courtesans because “it is impossible to avoid disease” among sex workers in other strata, the authors showed little concern for sex workers’ welfare.

In contrast, mainstream newspapers frequently depicted sex workers as “poor, oppressed, exploited, often battered” streetwalkers trafficked into the industry by their madams. This portrayal was in line with a broader social campaign against the sex industry, which was seen as a retrograde vice on par with foot-binding, gambling, and opium smoking.

This was the image of sex work that eventually came to dominate in modern China: “Stories of attractive, entrepreneurial, successful, socially and geographically mobile prostitutes” were overtaken by a narrative of “litigation, violence, victimization, medicalization, and taxation.”

After coming to power in 1949, the new Communist government drew on the language of “social illness” in its effort to re-educate sex workers and eradicate sex work.

“Continually obscured in all of this are the voices of the prostitutes themselves—voices which, while surely not unified, given the variety of arrangements under which women sold sexual services, certainly would sound different,” Hershatter writes. Behind the competing images of glamour and exploitation were women whose own stories have largely been lost to history.

item.title: London’s Railway for the Dead
item.dc:creator: Amelia Soth
item.description:
As London's graveyards overflowed, a private company proposed a remarkable new way to bury the dead.

The post London’s Railway for the Dead appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
item.content:encoded:
The final journey for London’s dead, circa 1860, was a trip on the London Necropolis Railway. The train would take the corpse and the accompanying mourners out of the city to the sprawling Brookwood Cemetery, where they had their pick of two stations: one for Anglicans, one for Non-Conformists. The deceased rode first, second, or third class (to avoid posthumous intermingling of rich and poor). But naturally, all coffin tickets were one way only.

Brookwood Cemetery was established in 1854 by the London Necropolis and National Mausoleum Company. Founded in response to a crisis of overcrowding in London’s churchyards, it was intended to hold all of London’s dead, for the rest of time—the vast majority of them in unmarked paupers’ graves.

Gravediggers forced as many bodies into one grave as they could, sometimes breaking apart the cadavers “with choppers and pickaxes” in order to make them fit.

At the time, the city’s population had grown far beyond what its existing patchwork of small graveyards could accommodate. Gravediggers forced as many bodies into one grave as they could, sometimes breaking apart the cadavers “with choppers and pickaxes” in order to make them fit. While they were at it, they could make a little extra cash by stripping down the old caskets to resell the handles and nails. Graves were reopened so often that the grass had no time to grow over them. Death was not dignified: the dearly departed lay in black mud scattered with litter.

A series of cholera epidemics, starting in 1832, turned the situation from an aesthetic nuisance into a serious health hazard. Rumors circulated about people who died gruesome deaths after simply breathing in the miasmatic vapors that rolled off an open grave.

In 1850, a new Burials Act banned the use of churchyards for future burials, necessitating a speedy solution for London’s dead. The very next year, the London Necropolis and National Mausoleum Company purchased a massive tract of land outside the city on a major rail line. Besides providing ample room, the company developed a cheap “earth-to-earth” coffin, made of biodegradable wood pulp, which would speed decomposition rather than allowing unwholesome vapours to linger.

Not everyone was a fan. The bishop of London, for one, was a firm opponent. He was concerned about the impropriety of a for-profit company dealing with the dead, and disturbed that all of London’s dead—however upstanding or immoral they may have been in life—would travel together on the same train, and wind up in the same final resting place. Nor was the clatter and bustle of a railway journey compatible, in his view, with the solemnity of a funeral.

More to Explore

A Mother Superior’s Demons

Amelia Soth
October 31, 2024
What does it mean when an entire convent of Urusline nuns appears to be possessed by demons? Many things, as it turns out.

Though the bishop didn’t say it, the cemetery represented a blow to the authority of the church. Burials had been a religious matter for centuries; the founding of privately owned, nondenominational cemeteries marked a massive shift away from the status quo. For the first time, people of all sects would be buried together; uniquely for its time, Brookwood Cemetery even had a section for people of the Zoroastrian faith.

Brookwood Cemetery was just one example of many in the burgeoning “garden cemetery” movement. The movement is usually traced back to Père Lachaise in Paris, established in 1804, although cemetery designer John Claudius Loudon cited the much older park-like cemeteries of Istanbul and Persia among his inspirations.

Garden cemeteries were suburban or rural landscapes designed to evoke rest and renewal. A visitor to one such garden cemetery exclaimed: “A glance at this beautiful cemetery almost excites a wish to die”—a far cry from the austere memento mori of a cluttered medieval churchyard. The new cemeteries were places of rest for the dead, but also places of leisure for the living.

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

The Victorian era was the golden age of mourning, the sentimental demands of the period driving an entire industry—from dark veils and jet-black jewelry to custom brooches woven from the dearly departed’s hair. As historian Cornelia D. J. Pearsall points out in her analysis of the Duke of Wellington’s funeral, Victorians were caught between two competing impulses: an “anxious repulsion of the dead,” which drove a series of public health reforms, and “a profound attachment to remains.” The dead are our dear ones—beloved friends and family, honored ancestors. At the same time, they are decaying matter—frightening, and perhaps even dangerous.

Today, London is once again running out of room for graves. The City of London Cemetery and Crematorium has begun to reuse the old ones—this time with a great deal more care and respect for the dead, both old and new. You can even reuse headstones: flip them around, and carve new names and dates on the back. In a city where burial space has always been precious, even the dead must make room for those who come after.

item.title: How Telepathy Helped Build the Russian Internet
item.dc:creator: The Editors
item.description:
During the Cold War, Soviet scientists pursued an unlikely way to communicate with the outside world.

The post How Telepathy Helped Build the Russian Internet appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
item.content:encoded:
Path to Open Books on JSTOR

Hacking the Iron Curtain: A Media Archaeology of the Russian Internet is part of JSTOR’s Path to Open initiative, which helps nonprofit university presses meet the challenges of open access publishing. Books in the program become open access three years after publication. JSTOR Daily is making the first and second chapters available for free now to drive awareness of the program.

On September 5, 1982, a music festival in San Bernardino, California, organized by Apple’s Steve Wozniak, bore witness to the first-ever public television link between the United States and the Soviet Union. Two large screens on either side of the stage broadcast performances by singer-songwriter Alla Pugacheva and rock band Voskreseniye, while Soviet citizens gathered at a Moscow radio station rocked out to the American lineup—that is, until Grateful Dead promoter Bill Graham, “convinced the whole thing was a KGB trick,” as Jeffrey Kripal wrote in his 2007 book Esalen: America and the Religion of No Religion, “literally pulled the plug halfway through the concert.”

This so-called US-Soviet Space Bridge (the first of several, including one co-hosted by television host Phil Donahue) often features in books about the cultural history of the Cold War. But what many of these books don’t tell you is that a large number of the people who organized these events also hoped to lift the Iron Curtain through another method: telepathy. In her new book Hacking the Iron Curtain: A Media Archaeology of the Russian Internet, journalist and “media archeologist” Natalia Konradova reveals how the story of the early Soviet internet—and the role it played during the collapse of the USSR in 1991—can be traced back to early- and mid-twentieth-century dreams of instantaneous and unmediated mass communication.

Telepathy was, for much of the twentieth century, considered a real possibility—one whose secrets modern science could and would eventually discover.

Though recognized today as a pseudoscientific fantasy, telepathy was, for much of the twentieth century, considered a real possibility—one whose secrets modern science could and would eventually discover. In the Soviet Union, scientific interest in telepathy stemmed not only from a sense of general techno-optimism shared by many countries both before and after the two world wars, but also from beliefs and aspirations particular to communist society. Like cosmism (a philosophical movement that aimed at nothing less than the colonization of space, the attainment of immortality, and the resurrection of every person who ever lived), research into “parapsychology” was expected to help usher in a utopian future.

Of course, what this future looked like depended on who you asked. Some scientists and science fiction authors envisioned a world in which doctors could diagnose patients remotely and one person could beam their skills and talents directly into the bodies of others. The CIA worried that Soviet officials would be able to steal sensitive government information and control “machines on the moon or in the ocean” with their thoughts, according to a 1973 report. Meanwhile, Iosif Goldin—a parapsychology enthusiast and principal organizer of the Soviet side of the first Space Bridge—imagined mass communication as a cure for geopolitical conflict. He once wrote that if “one realizes the observation of the sunrise simultaneously on all continents of the Earth and does it regularly, turning it into a form of bringing people together, there may be no nuclear catastrophe.”

Although the internet itself did not directly contribute to the USSR’s demise, it should come as no surprise that the appearance of one closely coincided with the disappearance of the other. Described by Konradova as a “perfected version of samizdat,” or self-published dissident literature, the rise of the internet and online communities made censorship and the suppression of information virtually impossible—at least for a time. Hacking the Iron Curtain concludes with a brief though warranted reflection on how, amid digital restrictions under Vladimir Putin, the Russian internet ecosystem—Runet—has become increasingly cut off from the rest of the World Wide Web, aiding the country’s return to autocracy.

How did you become interested in parapsychology?

I have worked on many different subjects as an anthropologist and media theorist. But I have always been particularly interested in phenomena or systems that are either created by users or shaped through their efforts and self-organization. It does not really matter whether I’m studying war memorials in small villages, which were one of the subjects I researched in the early 2000s, or internet literature—a phenomenon of the early Russian internet, when users had for the first time the opportunity to publish their literary works without them having to pass through any editorial process.

That was how my research into the Russian-speaking internet began. In the mid-2000s, colleagues in Germany invited me to join their project, where I studied internet forums. At that point, though, neither cybernetics nor parapsychology was anywhere on my research horizon. They emerged only during the research process.

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

What did you feel was missing from existing treatments of this subject (like Alaina Lemon’s book) that you wanted to explore with Hacking the Iron Curtain?

Because my research is interdisciplinary, I read literature from a wide range of research fields: the history of the internet and digital culture, Cold War studies, studies of utopias and technological imaginaries, “parascience,” and so on. These fields have been studied for a long time, and each has produced fascinating work. What I felt was missing was precisely the connection between them.

Alaina Lemon’s book was an important discovery for me, not only because it was the only work I encountered that placed Soviet parapsychology within the context of the Cold War, but also because she shows just how powerful the mutual desire for communication was among people in both the USSR and the US. That said, Lemon’s approach was grounded more in theatrical practices, and she was not interested in the history of technology. When Soviet parapsychology is discussed elsewhere, it is typically situated within the history of supernatural beliefs and esoteric practices, as in The New Age of Russia: Occult and Esoteric Dimensions, a substantial volume edited by Birgit Menzel.

What interested me was a phenomenon identified in the 1960s by Lynn Schroeder and Sheila Ostrander, authors of the classic Psychic Discoveries Behind the Iron Curtain: for a considerable period in the USSR, parapsychology was treated as a science. Researchers used scientific methods in their experiments and attempted to identify patterns in telepathy, telekinesis, and other phenomena. Yes, this no longer fits within our contemporary scientific understanding of the world, but I am talking about events that took place sixty years ago, when faith in the power of science was virtually limitless. As far as I know, before my work, no one had considered research into telepathy as one scientific field among others—regarded today as a dead end, but one that at the time could be seen as almost equivalent in status to computer science.

At what stage in your research did it become clear to you that there was a connection between parapsychology—telepathy in particular—and the early Russian internet?

I originally set out to study the history of the Russian internet. I interviewed figures from the Runet of the 1990s and worked with online archives. In those archives, I discovered that one of Russia’s first internet providers had actually been founded in the 1980s. This simply did not fit with my understanding that the internet could only have appeared after the collapse of the USSR in 1991.

Once I delved into the history of the first network connections from Soviet territory, I found myself dealing with an entirely new set of questions and, for me, an entirely new research field. Media archaeology is exactly the kind of (proto) discipline that is interested in dead ends, unrealized projects, and strange coincidences. It is still not particularly well known in the US, but I live in Germany, the birthplace of media archaeology.

To what extent was parapsychology research responsible for the rise of the Russian internet?

I distinguish between several levels of this connection. One is relatively simple and straightforward. The first contact between American and Soviet users on Usenet became possible thanks to American entrepreneur Joel Schatz, who came to the USSR in the mid-1980s. He did so because of his connections to the Esalen Institute in California, a well-known center of “alternative research,” now better known as a popular retreat destination for California tech people.

Esalen, in turn, had those connections because people associated with the institute had begun traveling to the USSR in the early 1970s hoping to establish contacts with Soviet parapsychologists (and they did). Later, they established a Soviet-American exchange program and joined the citizen-diplomacy movement, but initially it was the parapsychologists—with their desire for grassroots communication and their refusal to accept conventional boundaries of what was possible—who proved capable of connecting people from two countries on opposing sides of the Cold War.

More to Explore

How Hacking Got Hacked

Livia Gershon
November 23, 2018
How the archetype of the quirky, brilliant tech entrepreneur whose ideas could change the world migrated from high-tech hacker culture to Wall Street.

While studying this phenomenon, I also arrived at another, conceptual level of connection. In a sense, the internet is telepathy, except that a digital signal plays the role of the brain waves that science has never succeeded in discovering. In the 1960s, an era of techno-optimism and great hopes that human reason would triumph over war, disease, and death, computer science and the development of computer networks advanced alongside research into other possible forms of communication—forms that do not exist in nature but that, theoretically, could exist.

You mention on multiple occasions that telepathy was researched more extensively in the USSR than elsewhere. Why was this?

I think the USSR, as a project intended to realize a socialist utopia—and I am not discussing here how successful that project ultimately proved to be—had much stronger investments in radical scientific discoveries expected to fundamentally transform human life. Some of these ambitions were realized, such as spaceflight. Scientists today are still working on others, such as immortality. Others, such as telepathy, have disappeared from the scientific agenda.

One could probably add that the USSR had an obvious overproduction of specialists in the natural sciences, which was connected to the military-industrial complex. At some point, the Soviet Ministry of Defense also began investing in this new field because it seemed potentially useful for defense purposes. As a result, Soviet laboratories could often find room for experiments involving new and uncertain phenomena.

Still, I think all of this was more a consequence of the first factor: an exceptionally strong belief in scientific progress. Both American and Soviet societies were modern societies, if by modernity we mean above all a reliance on rational knowledge and technology. But in the USSR, this modernity was particularly radical and allowed virtually no alternative: it lay at the very foundation of the state as the only possible form of its existence.

You mention that Soviet scientists like Vladimir Bekhterev continued to research telepathy even after failing to find proof of its existence. Why did this interest persist, including among the CIA and US politicians?

In general, I have the impression that, from the 1920s through the end of the 1980s, scientists around the world were reluctant to abandon the subject completely. I do not know enough about Bekhterev’s activities to speculate confidently about his motives, but I do know that he was aware of the research his former student Vasiliev was conducting at his institute. I interpret this as an attempt not to burn any bridges—simply to keep the possibility open, “just in case.” What if the experiments ultimately did produce results, and you found yourself among those accused of suppressing something new and progressive? But of course, that is only my theory.

As for the CIA and politicians, that belongs to a different period. Judging from documents in the declassified CIA archives, they were deeply impressed by reports of Soviet achievements in this field and wrote alarmed assessments suggesting that the USSR might soon learn to guide missiles with the power of thought, kill people with a glance, and so on. Their primary objective, therefore, was to ensure the United States did not fall behind in this area.

Beyond parapsychology, to what extent did the Soviet internet become possible thanks to perestroika, and to what extent did perestroika become possible thanks to the Soviet internet?

I do not think I would subscribe to either proposition, because for me the causal relationship lies outside both perestroika and the Soviet internet. Rather, a second modernity—or postmodernity—arrived: a period in which users gained real possibilities to influence events. In the USSR, perestroika began, and contacts with the US intensified. In the United States, the internet became available to a critical mass of users. The mythology of the Cold War was ceasing to work on both sides: people understood that official authorities were lying and wanted to escape their control. All of this was happening simultaneously.

Of course, before perestroika, it would have been impossible for an American to walk into a closed Soviet scientific institute and ask to be connected to a classified network—which is exactly what happened when the internet provider SovAm Teleport was founded in the mid-1980s. But perestroika itself would not have happened if a significant portion of Soviet society had not already been ready for it.

You note that, at various points in twentieth-century Soviet history, techno-utopian dreams often gave way to practical and commercial applications. Between the two, which ultimately plays a larger role in this story?

Once connecting to the internet from the USSR became technically possible, there was much less room for fantasy. Why take risks and invest in uncertainty—which any grand vision requires—when a concrete technical solution already exists, and all you need is the money to implement it? More broadly, the USSR was shifting from overregulated socialism to unregulated capitalism, which would reveal itself in full force in the 1990s.

Nevertheless, pragmatism and commerce alone did not define the character of the early Russian internet. Because early users saw the network primarily as a hobby, they enthusiastically invested their time and energy in games, poetry, and all kinds of impractical inventions. Until the end of the 1990s, when the first major commercial projects emerged, the network was primarily a space for entertainment and free communication.

Can you talk about the role Russian Usenet played during and after the unsuccessful 1991 coup attempt to prevent the USSR from collapsing? Could events have played out differently if Russians had not had this window to the outside world?

This was an important moment. Information about the Moscow coup of 1991 reached American media and politicians largely through Usenet users at the Kurchatov Institute, in Moscow. They, in turn, collected information through their internal network, translated it into English, and posted it to newsgroups.

I would say the absence of the internet probably would not have changed the fundamental course of events, because the victory of the democratic forces during the coup depended much more on resistance on the ground than on support from other countries. The absence of access to Usenet might, however, have affected more specific aspects of what happened: how quickly information circulated, how much pressure came from outside the Soviet Union, and so on.

Some people think that if the Soviet internet had developed sooner, it could have ensured the survival of the USSR. Do you share this belief?

The idea that the development of the internet might have saved the USSR comes from the author of an alternate-history novel in which technologies are transported into the Soviet Union from the future. I don’t believe in this idea, because creating the internet required not only high-quality materials, which were in short supply, but also international cooperation, from which the USSR was cut off after World War II. It also required the internet itself—if, by the internet, we mean a system of communication and community formation.

I think this last factor matters most. Soviet society, and even more so the Soviet leadership, had absolutely no need for people to communicate freely with one another beyond institutional control. At the same time, Soviet engineers were already connecting computers into networks before work on ARPANET had even begun. In other words, the technical possibility existed, but neither the social demand nor the political will did. Even telephone services remained unavailable in many Soviet cities until the 1990s. To stay in touch, people exchanged letters, postcards, and telegrams.

More to Explore

The Chilean Wide Web?

Matthew Wills
July 23, 2022
Salvador Allende’s attempt to network the national economy mirrored his government’s struggle to balance centralization and decentralization.

Cybernetics, however, did produce a powerful vision that extended far beyond computers and even beyond communication itself. But because cybernetics was a product of Soviet culture as a whole, that vision faded when Soviet culture entered into crisis. The desire to imagine radically different futures was replaced by a desire to “live like people in the West,” particularly in terms of everyday life and living standards.

In the conclusion, you draw parallels between the futurism of Silicon Valley (specifically the quest for immortality) and the techno-utopianism of Soviet cyberneticians. Could you also speak to any meaningful differences between these visions?

To be honest, there are surprisingly few substantial differences, and that amazes me. Eternal life is hardly a new idea, of course, but one might still expect to see signs that these people lived in different periods and in very different cultures.

One possible distinction is that the American version of this techno-utopia is somewhat less closely tied to the public good and more oriented toward individual benefit, whereas Soviet cyberneticians had in mind, first and foremost, a new society, and only then a new human being as a member of that society. But we also have to remember that Soviet cyberneticians wrote articles and gave interviews under conditions of censorship. With that in mind, this difference may be less substantial than it initially appears.

In your conclusion, you write that the “historical connection between the attempts to rebuild the power lost during the collapse of the USSR and the current reality cannot be ignored.” To what extent did the Russian internet contribute to Russian world ideology and its consequences, including the war in Ukraine?

The figures of the early Russian internet did not make the decision to launch a military attack on Ukraine, and they should not be held responsible for it. The concept of the “Russian World” emerged from the political technologies of the late 1990s and early 2000s. Although political technologists participated in the development of the Russian internet, they were not the ones who made the decision to launch Russia’s most recent military aggression.

Nevertheless, I do see—and describe in the book—a conceptual connection between the expansive space of Russian-language verbal culture, which became the first meaningful content of the Russian-speaking internet, and the “Russian World.” The fact that this connection is conceptual is important.

Until very recently, the expression “Russian internet” was something of an oxymoron, because the internet is, by definition, a global network. Yes, you can write in any language you like, but technically you are still writing on a common, international internet that does not recognize state borders. This is no longer entirely the case. In Russia, a “sovereign Runet” whose borders increasingly coincide with the state’s borders has, by now, almost become a reality.

In other words, Russians first entered the American internet; then they developed the concept of the “Runet,” which technically remained part of the global network but was culturally understood as a unique and independent phenomenon; and decades later, they physically carved out a segment of the global network in which international conventions no longer operate in the same way and where an antiwar post can result in a prison sentence. I am not sure I would call this a “Sonderweg,” but it is a remarkable development. One can only hope that the rest of the world will not follow the same path, although there are reasons for concern.

item.title: Mental Hospitals at the Movies
item.dc:creator: Livia Gershon
item.description:
The horror films of the 1970s captured a cultural shift from fears of institutional abuse to anxieties about psychiatric patients living freely.

The post Mental Hospitals at the Movies appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
item.content:encoded:
Psychiatric facilities and their patients have long been fodder for horror stories. As historian Troy Rondinone writes, films of the 1970s harnessed and shaped the American public’s understanding of deinstitutionalization and its aftermath.

Rondinone writes that the downsizing and closure of many state mental hospitals between the 1950s and 1970s were partly driven by the wider availability of low-cost antipsychotic medications and partly by efforts to save money. But another factor was growing public concern about the human cost of involuntary commitment, institutional abuse, and ineffective treatment.

Instead of building better systems of community care, federal, state, and local governments had largely abandoned individuals who had previously been institutionalized in psychiatric hospitals.

The Exorcist (1973) presented medical institutions as helpless to address the real problems of madness. When Jesuit priest Damien Karras visits Bellevue Hospital, the institution is shown in a depressing and frightening light familiar to the public from exposés of mental hospitals over the previous three decades. Regan, the possessed little girl, is saved only when Father Karras abandons modern medicine for religion.

Two years later, Rondinone writes, One Flew over the Cuckoo’s Nest (1975) reflected the era’s cynicism toward government, depicting an individual caught in a dehumanizing institution. Jack Nicholson played the protagonist R. P. McMurphy as a gleeful, anti-authority trickster. The film drew on existing tropes about authoritarianism generally and mental hospitals specifically. It portrayed treatments that were already outdated by the film’s 1963 setting—intensely painful electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and lobotomy—to dramatize the inhumanity of the system.

More to Explore

Selling Slashers to Teen Girls

Livia Gershon
September 25, 2019
The heroines of 1970s and 80s teen horror movies were traditionally feminine, tough, and sexually confident.

By the late 1970s, though, public understanding of mental health issues was changing. Deinstitutionalization hadn’t gone as many self-advocates with mental illness had hoped. Instead of building better systems of community care, federal, state, and local governments had largely abandoned individuals who had previously been institutionalized in psychiatric hospitals. In the media and political discourse, discussion of mental illness began to center on unhoused people and the danger they supposedly posed to others.

Against this backdrop, Rondinone writes, Halloween (1978) and When a Stranger Calls (1979) both portrayed people who had escaped from psychiatric hospitals as monstrous killers. The institution that Halloween’s villain, Michael Myers, escapes from is shown not as a place of healing or a site of authoritarian domination of the innocent, but as a prison where medications are used primarily to subdue monsters.

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

In When a Stranger Calls, a psychiatrist at the mental hospital from which child-killer Curt Duncan escaped explains that Duncan received effective, if unpleasant, treatment—including tranquilizers, lithium, and 38 rounds of ECT. But these treatments prove all in vain. Duncan ends up on the streets, where he is beaten and later seen nervously muttering to himself. Ultimately, he resumes his irrationally murderous behavior.

Neither film advocates a return to institutionalization. Instead, they reflect a cynicism about mental hospitals—and a rejection of any humanistic hope for the rehabilitation of people with mental illness. Rondinone writes that this shift was part of a turn toward a Reagan-era cinematic world in which individuals must confront unpredictable dangers without hope of government support or protection. In these films, the horrors of institutionalization gave way to the horrors of a world without it.
